model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Backgammon game. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(state: dict) -> str: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - Your `policy` receives a single Python dict named `state` with the following keys: - - `state['my_pts']`: a length-24 list of nonnegative integers giving how many of your checkers are on each point. - - `state['opp_pts']`: a length-24 list of nonnegative integers giving how many opponent checkers are on each point. - - `state['my_bar']`: number of your checkers on the bar (waiting to re-enter). - - `state['opp_bar']`: number of opponent checkers on the bar. - - `state['my_off']`: number of your checkers borne off (scored). - - `state['opp_off']`: number of opponent checkers borne off (scored). - - `state['dice']`: a list of 0, 1, or 2 integers in `1..6` representing the current roll (e.g., `[5, 6]`). - Point indices are absolute indices `0..23` as used by the engine: - - `0` and `23` are the extreme points (endpoints) of the board; You always move from `23` to `0` while your opponent moves from `0` to `23`, this is handled by the engine. - - You do not need to compute destinations; your action specifies only the starting points for up to two checker moves. - Legal-move constraints are enforced by the engine, including: - - If you have any checkers on the bar, you must move them before moving other checkers. - - You may not move onto a point occupied by 2 or more opposing checkers. - - If only one die can be played, you must play the higher die when possible. - - If both dice can be played, you must play both. - - Bearing off is only allowed when all of your remaining checkers are in your home board (A0..A5). # Action / Return Format - Return a move string in the fixed compact format: `:,` with no spaces. - `` is one character: `H` or `L`. - - `H` means the first encoded checker move uses the higher die. - - `L` means the first encoded checker move uses the lower die. - `` and `` are the start locations for the first and second checker moves. - Each `` token must be one of: - - `A0`..`A23` for an absolute point index (0..23). - - `B` for Bar. - - `P` for Pass (no checker move). - Examples: - - `H:A0,A18` means: apply the higher die from point 0, and the lower die from point 18. - - `L:B,A5` means: apply the lower die from Bar, then the higher die from point 5. - - `H:P,P` means: no legal moves (full pass). - The move string must correspond to a legal action for the current state and dice. - Do not care about hit markers, destinations, or parentheses; hits and end points are computed for you by the engine. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I need to design a Backgammon policy that outputs legal moves in the compact format, which means working through the state representation, movement direction, and generating all legal moves while respecting bar rules, the higher-die rule, using both dice, and bearing off. Since I move from point 23 toward 0, my home board spans A0 through A5, and bearing off happens when a point minus the die value goes below zero.

The opponent moves in the opposite direction, from 0 to 23, with their home in points 18 through 23. I'm working out how the state dictionary represents checker counts for each side, and how bar entry works -- my checkers re-enter through the opponent's home board using point 24 minus the die value.

Doubles are tricky since the action format only supports two checker moves, but standard backgammon allows four moves with doubles. I need to figure out how the engine handles this simplification, possibly by only allowing two moves per turn even on doubles, or by calling the policy again with the same roll.

I'm also considering edge cases where the dice list has fewer than two values, meaning only one move (or a pass) might be needed. Since I don't know the exact legality rules the engine enforces, I want to build a thorough legal-move generator that tries both dice orderings, handles bar entries first when checkers are on the bar, and falls back to passing when no legal move exists for a given die.

I'll implement the standard rule for single-die moves, keeping the lower die first when only one die is playable, and for doubles just use "H" since order doesn't matter. For bearing off, I'm coding the standard exact-or-highest-point legality check.

Now I'm thinking through the evaluation heuristic — starting with pip count difference and blot exposure, weighting penalties by how many opponent checkers could hit each exposed blot.

I'll also account for made points and primes (especially in the home board), bonuses for hitting opponent blots and holding anchors in their home, plus progress on bearing off. When the position becomes a pure race with no contact, I'll switch to evaluating purely by pip count and bear-off efficiency, avoiding checker stacking and wasted pips, while also considering prime structures and how many entry points I deny the opponent when they're on the bar.

Given the 1-second budget, I'm estimating the move generation cost — roughly 450 candidate first/second die combinations with cheap evaluations, which should be fast enough, and I'm considering whether a shallow lookahead over opponent responses is feasible.

I decide full 21-roll opponent expansion is too costly in Python within 1 second, so I'll fold hitting risk directly into the static evaluator instead, using shot-probability tables based on blot distances. Now I'm working out the exact geometry of hitting: since my checkers move high-to-low and the opponent's move low-to-high, a hit occurs when an opponent checker's point is less than my blot's point, with distance equal to their difference, and bar checkers entering via die value need to be factored into this the same way.

Now I'm laying out the standard shot-probability table by distance out of 36 rolls, but recognizing it ignores blocked points, so I'm considering a more accurate method: for each blot, iterate over the 21 distinct rolls and check whether the opponent's move is actually legal given my blocking points, which is still cheap enough to compute directly rather than approximating.

I'm also weighing how to combine multiple blots being hittable at once—whether to take the max cost among hittable blots per roll or sum contributions—and I'm working out the entry rules when the opponent has checkers on the bar, since with two on the bar both dice must be used to enter and a hit only counts if the entry point lands exactly on my blot.

Direct hits require a source point exactly one die away from the blot (or a bar checker entering there), while combined hits using both dice need the intermediate landing point to be open and, if the opponent has one checker on the bar, that checker must enter first before the second die can be used to complete the hit.

For doubles, I'm uncertain whether the engine treats them as allowing more than two moves per turn. Since overestimating risk is safer than underestimating it, I'll consider distances up to 4a for doubles rather than limiting to 2a.

Now I'm working out evaluation features from my own perspective: computing pip counts for both sides by summing checker positions plus bar checkers weighted at 25, then checking whether contact still exists between the two sides based on the relative positions of my rearmost checker and the opponent's frontmost checker.

For pure races, I'll base the score mainly on the pip differential (opponent's pips minus mine), with a bonus for bearing off checkers and a slight penalty for checkers still outside the home board, keeping the formula simple. For contact positions I still need to work out the weighting scheme.

For blot risk, I want to calculate the cost of getting hit at a given point as the pip loss plus a penalty scaled by how many home-board points the opponent already controls, since a stronger opponent home board makes re-entry harder. I also plan to reward made points, giving extra weight to points inside my own home board and mid-board points that help build a prime.

Now I'm thinking about how a prime's value depends on trapping opponent checkers behind it — the bonus should only kick in if the opponent actually has checkers stuck behind the blockade, scaling roughly with prime length squared. I still need to work out how to value anchors.

My anchors deep in the opponent's home (their 5-point and bar-point) are valuable for safety, so I'm re-deriving indices from the opponent's perspective (their pip count for a checker at index j is 24-j, meaning their bar-point sits at index 17, their 5-point at index 19). I want to penalize having too many back checkers late in the game or leaving a lone back checker exposed, while rewarding sending the opponent to the bar — especially scaled by how many home-board points I already hold — and giving a small bonus for blots I could hit next turn. I still need to work out the stacking penalty for too many checkers piled on one point.

I'm also weighing penalties for checkers stranded on deep points (0,1,2) early in the game while contact still exists, a bonus for checkers already borne off, and skipping gammon-specific scoring for now. For opponent blots, I'll add a modest bonus based on my hit probability using a simple distance table rather than a full pip-count simulation, and I'm calibrating rough weights where a pip is the base unit, being hit costs roughly the pip loss plus tempo, and a made home point is worth about 5-8 pips. I also need to make sure checkers still on the bar after my move are handled correctly by treating them as 25 pips.

Now I'm working out a containment feature: penalizing my back checkers when they sit behind opponent-made points within the six spaces ahead of them, scaled by how many checkers are trapped and how strong the opposing block is, and treating this symmetrically with the prime bonus I already have for blocking the opponent. I'm also planning a large bonus for when the opponent is stuck on the bar against a closed six-point home board, and need to handle the backgammon rule requiring the higher die to be played when only one die is usable.

Writing move application logic...

I'm defining how legal moves work for entering from the bar, moving within the board, and bearing off, including hit detection when landing on a single opposing checker, then generating all valid two-die move sequences by trying both dice orders and tracking cases where only one die can be played.

For cases where dice are forced (partial moves), I'll prioritize playing the higher die if that's the only option available, falling back to formats like "H:P,P" when no moves exist, and I'm also handling single-die and no-dice edge cases, deduplicating resulting states by comparing final board tuples for efficiency.

Now I'm working through the hit probability logic - for each of the 21 possible dice rolls, I need to check which of my blot positions the opponent could reach given their checker locations and bar count, factoring in direct hits, combined-die hits, and blocked intermediate points.

For opponent checkers on the bar (1 or 2), I need special handling for entry combined with hitting, including cases where the entering checker itself lands on or passes through my blot, and doubles allowing multiple entry attempts.

For the cost of a blot, I want it to reflect distance, tempo loss, and the strength of the opponent's home board, since being hit against a closed board is far worse than against a weak one. I'll estimate risk as a weighted sum over all rolls of the cost of the worst (and partially second-worst) exposed blot, then move to assessing my own hitting chances against the opponent symmetrically.

I realize I can reuse the same hit-risk logic for both directions by mirroring the board so the attacker always moves in the same conceptual direction, feeding in defender points, attacker points, and attacker bar count accordingly. I'll weight my own hitting chances lower than the risk to me, since the opponent moves first and might cover their blot.

Given roughly 450 candidate positions and two risk calculations each, this should stay well under a second in practice, though I want to be efficient and only evaluate blots that actually have an attacker sitting behind them, plus dedupe final positions to avoid wasted work.

For the race-only case with no contact, I'm thinking through a scoring formula based on pip count difference, checkers already borne off, and penalties for checkers still outside the home board or awkward bear-off stacking.

Now I'm sketching the general contact scoring formula: pip count difference between opponent and me, weighted bonuses for checkers already borne off on each side, and a term subtracting my expected exposure to being hit.

I'm also assigning point values across the board (my points, bar point, midpoint, and opponent's home points as potential anchors), and I'm considering scaling those home-point values based on how many opponent checkers are trapped behind my blockade or on the bar.

I'm also adding scoring for prime formation bonuses, penalties for opponent checkers on the bar facing a strong home board, dancing risk from my own bar checkers, stacking and dead-checker penalties, and penalties for back checkers trapped behind multiple opponent points.

I'm mirroring the trap logic with an escape/trapping bonus for opponent checkers stuck behind my made points, adding specific back-checker and anchor penalties/bonuses, and noting that blot risk in my home board against an opponent checker on the bar is already covered by the general risk term, while race-ahead situations naturally favor safety through that same risk penalty.

Now I'm writing the move generation logic that handles bar entries, blocked entry checks, and hit detection when landing on opponent blots.

Writing move legality code...

Still writing policy logic...

I'm double-checking the higher-die-must-be-played rule, deduping states with a cache keyed by board tuples, and now sketching a pip-count based evaluation function comparing my pips against the opponent's.

In the race branch, I'm factoring in bear-off count differences, penalizing checkers outside the home board, and discouraging stacking too many checkers on a single point — though I'm realizing the pip count already captures some of this and I need to reconsider whether checkers on point 6 versus 8 matter beyond raw pips for bearing off efficiently.

For contact positions, I'm now designing a hit-risk function: it identifies blots, filters out ones with no attacking checker positioned to threaten them, checks which points are blocked (two or more defenders), then loops through all dice roll combinations to tally which blots are hittable and their associated risk cost.

I'm working out the can_hit logic separately -- direct shots, combination shots for non-doubles, and multi-step doubles sequences, and now extending it to handle the entering-from-the-bar cases where one or two dice are needed to re-enter before hitting.

Finishing the edge case handling for entry points and blocked intermediates, then moving to defining a cost function for exposed blots — weighting distance from home along with tempo penalties based on how many checkers the opponent has in their home board.

For threats against opponent blots, I'm mirroring that same cost logic but weighting it lower since it's the opponent's move next, giving them a chance to escape first. Now I'm defining point values for the board layout to weight positional importance...

Anchors get valued by depth—the golden anchor at opponent's five-point highest, tapering down toward their one-point. I'm also scaling a multiplier based on how many opponent checkers remain trapped behind my blocking points, since those points matter far less if the opponent's back checkers have already escaped.

I'm penalizing having too many checkers stacked on the anchor or too many checkers back overall, then writing a loop to detect made points that block opponent checkers still stuck behind them.

I also want a prime-consecutive bonus for runs of three or more made points, and I'm weighing whether the existing blocking count already captures enough of that effect. And I should factor in the opponent's bar checkers when scoring hits.

I'm also adding penalties for stacking too many checkers on a single point when in contact, extra penalties for deep points near the back, and a small bonus rewarding flexibility across distinct occupied points.

Skipping distribution bonus for now — blots not currently reachable by the opponent shouldn't count as risk, and that filtering seems to be handled correctly already. I'm noting that blots which could become hittable later aren't penalized, which seems acceptable, then moving on to consider factors from the opponent's side.

Hitting an opponent's blot deep in my home board only gains a few pips, but the cost formula already accounts for this through the mirrored position calculation. For contact-mode evaluation, when I have checkers borne off while the opponent still has a checker back, I want to add a bonus for my own borne-off checkers and reward making points in my home board, since that encourages good structural play during contact.

Now I'm verifying the starting position setup, mapping each player's checkers to their correct indices, and confirming that the mirrored indices for the opponent's points match up correctly. Then I check the standard opening move for a 3-1 roll, which should bring checkers down to make the 5-point.

For the 6-5 opening, "lover's leap" moves the back checker straight to the midpoint, so I'm evaluating pip equivalence versus alternatives and considering exposure risk from the blot left behind — factoring in tempo cost and shot distances from possible opponent attacking points.

Factoring in overlap on the hit numbers gets that risk down to about 4.5, though stacking six checkers on the midpoint carries a small penalty too. Overall, running to the midpoint still looks like the safer play.

Performance-wise, evaluating roughly 300 unique states with pip counts and risk checks should stay well within budget, maybe 60ms total. I still need to make sure edge cases with checkers on the bar and specific dice rolls are handled correctly.

I'm also double-checking bear-off rules with the higher die when higher points are empty, and confirming the standard "must play higher die" nuance matches what the engine expects, along with edge notations like "L:A5,P".

I'll go with putting the move first, like "L:A5,P", since the letter denotes which die the first encoded checker move uses—here the lower die plays A5, and the pass represents the unused higher die. That seems like the most natural convention.

For doubles, I'm reasoning that if the engine gives four moves via two calls, the second call likely repeats the same dice pair, and if doubles are represented as a single integer, that just resolves to one move per call. I'll set aside the single-die edge case for now and focus on how to evaluate among candidate partial moves.

Now I'm writing the full implementation: setting up dice roll combinations, point values for made points, legal move generation, applying moves, and an evaluation function based on pip counts and blot exposure...

Writing pip and evaluation logic...

Thinking through a bear-off example with checkers at 5 and 3 using a 6-2 roll, comparing bearing off versus repositioning — reasoning that the bear-off bonus should favor actually removing checkers when pip counts are otherwise equivalent.

Now I'm writing the function to count home board points and opponent home board points for contact evaluation.

Adding scaling for point values...

I'm scoring bar checkers, weighting captures more heavily against a stronger home board, and then computing a blocking bonus for opponent checkers trapped behind a chain of made points.

Adding blocking penalty for my rear checkers, then sanity-checking the calculation with a specific index example to confirm the math works out.

I'm now adding a penalty for excess back checkers beyond two, plus an extra liability penalty for a lone back checker without an anchor, reasoning that three-plus checkers deep is moderately bad early in the game. Moving on to think through stacking penalties for deep points...

Adding stack penalties...

Now working through prime-building logic, tracking consecutive made points to find the longest run.

Still computing risk exposure...

I'm double-checking the mirrored coordinate math for the attacker's entry point and the defender's blot exposure, making sure the index conversion (23 minus p, 24 minus d) lines up correctly with the real board positions.

I should guard against edge cases where the attacker has no checkers left, returning zero risk safely. The risk value is expressed in pip-equivalent units, so I need to weigh a blot's exposure cost against the probability of being hit and compare that against the value of making a point instead. I also need to factor in the pip gain from hitting an opponent's checker when deciding whether a hit is worthwhile.

opp_off stays constant across my candidate moves so it doesn't matter, but I'll include it anyway. Bearing off checkers naturally reduces my pip count, which is good, and I don't need any randomness for tie-breaking since deterministic scoring is fine. I should wrap the whole evaluation in a try/except with a fallback to picking a simple legal move in case something goes wrong.

Now I'm making sure the fallback itself only picks from legal candidates: I'll generate candidates first with straightforward logic, then wrap only the scoring/evaluation step in try/except, defaulting to the first candidate on failure. I'm also double-checking my bear-off legality check — confirming "all home" requires no checkers on points 6-23 and no checkers on the bar, and that for destinations past the board edge there must be no checkers on higher points. I'm also confirming the engine's rule that both dice must be played when possible, which my generator already prioritizes, and noting that doubles still only allow the standard move format so there's no special four-move action to handle.

I'm writing a function to estimate hit risk given board state, checker positions on the bar, and tempo — it finds the attacker's rearmost checker, identifies blot targets on the defender's side (adjusting logic depending on whether the attacker has checkers on the bar), then loops through all dice roll combinations weighting by probability, checking whether each blot can be hit and accumulating a weighted risk score based on pip distance and tempo, favoring the highest-value hit while adding partial credit for additional hits.

Now I'm verifying the hitting logic for combination rolls when checkers start on the bar, making sure intermediate landing squares aren't blocked by two or more of my own checkers, and confirming doubles cases (using 2, 3, or 4 of the same die) are handled correctly alongside the direct single-die hit case. I'm also checking edge cases — checkers already on the bar aren't counted as hittable blots, and bar-entry requirements are properly reflected when computing threats in both directions.

I'm structuring the policy function with a try/except wrapper that falls back to a simpler candidate generator, and ultimately to a hardcoded safe move if everything else fails. Writing the candidate generator...

Still writing move generation logic...

I record full sequences when both dice moves succeed, otherwise fall back to partial moves, preferring 'H' order results if available, and returning empty if nothing is legal at all. I'm double-checking the doubles case edge condition where only 'H' order partials exist, and now considering whether the higher die order matters for non-doubles rolls.

Then the policy needs to evaluate each resulting unique board state and pick the maximum value, factoring in that it's now the opponent's turn and adjusting for exposure risk. I'm also checking edge cases in the evaluation for bearing off with an opponent anchor still in my home board, and how bonuses and risk penalties interact there.

I'm confirming the contact detection logic — if the opponent has a checker on the bar, contact always exists since I have checkers still in play; and in race mode, contact is false only when all my checkers sit strictly ahead of all the opponent's, meaning neither side can hit. I'm also working through the outside-home penalty for race scoring with a concrete example roll, checking how moving checkers home affects that penalty.

I'm also checking that bearing off versus moving gives consistent pip-count results when both are legal options for a given roll, using specific checker positions as a test case. Everything checks out, so I'll add a small tiebreaker rule: if two moves score equally, just pick the first one.

For pip weighting in contact positions, structure matters more than raw pip count, so I'm valuing pips at 1.0 each versus 2-8 for positional points, since a hit typically gains 15-20 pips and strongly favors hitting under the "when in doubt, hit" principle—though I need to weigh that against the risk of exposing a blot to a strong return shot.

I'm also refining the prime/blocking bonus to count opponent checkers trapped behind my highest point, which matters for anchored opponents deep in my home board, and tracking opponent checkers near the bar for multiplier purposes.

Writing the hit-detection function...

That checks out - direct entry hits aren't blocked since the destination isn't occupied yet. I'm now writing the final code, including a token helper for identifying bar vs point positions and confirming the single-die path reuses the same evaluation logic, plus verifying the move application correctly updates positions and detects hits.
